summary.text: Using the rational bounds \(1.11803<\sqrt{5/4}<1.11804\) to determine the required floors gives \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). Thus at \(n=140\) the proposed right-hand side is \(528+484-471=541\), not \(542\), providing a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating both sides at \(n=140\).

Set
\[
x=\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
We first obtain exact rational bounds for \(x\):
\[
\frac{111803}{100000}<x<\frac{111804}{100000}.
\]
Indeed, all the quantities involved are positive, so these inequalities can be proved by squaring. For the lower bound,
\[
111803^2=12{,}499{,}910{,}809
   <12{,}500{,}000{,}000
   =\frac54\,100000^2.
\]
Thus \((111803/100000)^2<5/4\), and hence \(111803/100000<x\). For the upper bound,
\[
111804^2=12{,}500{,}134{,}416
   >12{,}500{,}000{,}000
   =\frac54\,100000^2.
\]
Thus \((111804/100000)^2>5/4\), and positivity gives \(x<111804/100000\).

We now use these bounds to determine the four irrational floor terms needed at indices \(140,144,157,161\). Recall that \(\lfloor y\rfloor=m\) exactly when \(m\le y<m+1\).

First, multiplying the rational bounds for \(x\) by \(140\) gives
\[
\frac{782621}{5000}<140x<\frac{195657}{1250}.
\]
The lower endpoint is greater than \(156\), since
\[
782621>156\cdot 5000=780000,
\]
and the upper endpoint is less than \(157\), since
\[
195657<157\cdot1250=196250.
\]
Consequently,
\[
156<140x<157,
\qquad	ext{so}\qquad
\lfloor140x\rfloor=156.
\]

Next, multiplication by \(144\) gives
\[
\frac{1006227}{6250}<144x<\frac{503118}{3125}.
\]
Here
\[
1006227>160\cdot6250=1000000
\]
and
\[
503118<161\cdot3125=503125.
\]
Therefore
\[
160<144x<161,
\qquad	ext{so}\qquad
\lfloor144x\rfloor=160.
\]

For \(157\), the same bounds give
\[
\frac{17553071}{100000}<157x<\frac{4388307}{25000}.
\]
The lower endpoint exceeds \(175\), because
\[
17553071>175\cdot100000=17500000,
\]
while the upper endpoint is below \(176\), because
\[
4388307<176\cdot25000=4400000.
\]
Thus
\[
175<157x<176,
\qquad	ext{so}\qquad
\lfloor157x\rfloor=175.
\]

Finally, multiplying by \(161\) gives
\[
\frac{18000283}{100000}<161x<\frac{4500111}{25000}.
\]
We have
\[
18000283>180\cdot100000=18000000
\]
and
\[
4500111<181\cdot25000=4525000.
\]
It follows that
\[
180<161x<181,
\qquad	ext{so}\qquad
\lfloor161x\rfloor=180.
\]

The remaining floor terms are ordinary integer divisions by \(4\):
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{140}{4}\right\rfloor=35,
\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{144}{4}\right\rfloor=36,
\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{157}{4}\right\rfloor=39,
\quad
\left\lfloor\frac{161}{4}\right\rfloor=40.
\]
(The third equality follows from \(157=4\cdot39+1\); the other three are immediate, with \(161=4\cdot40+1\).)

Substitution into the defining formula for the sequence now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(140)&=2\cdot140+156+35=471,\\
a(144)&=2\cdot144+160+36=484,\\
a(157)&=2\cdot157+175+39=528,\\
a(161)&=2\cdot161+180+40=542.
\end{aligned}
\]

If the conjectured recurrence held for every \(n\ge1\), then at \(n=140\) it would require
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
But the calculated right-hand side is
\[
528+484-471=541,
\]
whereas the left-hand side is
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the proposed equality becomes \(542=541\), which is false. Therefore the conjectured recurrence does not hold for every \(n\ge1\); \(n=140\) is a counterexample.
